sections.title: Prerequisite Review: Determinants as Area
sections.content: Briefly define the determinant of a 2x2 matrix as the 'signed area' of a parallelogram formed by the column vectors (a, b) and (c, d). Visualize this as a transformation of the unit square.
sections.example: Visualize the vector pair [2, 0] and [0, 2] creating a square with area 4. The determinant is 4.

sections.title: Framing the System as Column Vectors
sections.content: Introduce the system Ax = b as a linear combination of columns: x(col1) + y(col2) = b. Explain that we are looking for the 'weights' x and y that scale the columns to reach the target point b.
sections.example: A delivery drone (target b) is powered by two propellers with thrust vectors v1 and v2. We need to find the power settings x and y to reach the target.

sections.title: Geometric Substitution (The 'Area-Ratio' Logic)
sections.content: Explain Cramer's Rule geometrically: Replacing a column vector with b creates a new parallelogram. The ratio of the area of this new parallelogram to the original determines the scalar needed to reach the target.
sections.example: Show an animation where replacing the 'x-axis' vector with the target vector 'b' creates a new shape. The ratio of its area to the original area gives the x-coordinate.

sections.title: Putting it Together: The Visual Formula
sections.content: Formalize the rule: x = Det(A_x) / Det(A). Explain that because areas scale linearly, the ratio of areas perfectly isolates the scalar we are searching for.
sections.example: Calculate x for a system: 2x + 1y = 5, 1x + 2y = 4. Use the visual area boxes to show how the division of the 'new' parallelogram area by the 'original' area results in x=2, y=1.

sections.title: Summary & Intuition Check
sections.content: Conclude by highlighting why this is powerful: It turns a 'searching for unknowns' problem into an 'area comparison' problem. Note the limitation: This only works when the determinant is non-zero (i.e., vectors aren't collinear).
sections.example: An animation of two vectors collapsing into a single line (determinant 0) to show why Cramer's rule fails when the 'parallelogram' has no area.
